p: Thank you, Council Member. Next up, Council Member Hankerson.
Thank you, Chair. I just have a couple of questions. I know you mentioned that you don't have an exhaustive list of precautionary measures that businesses can take. Is that correct?
Council Member, thank you so much for the question. So, I think you're asking if we have a list of measures businesses take before retail theft incidents happen to protect themselves?

Correct. Well, just going back to Intro. 623, I see it listed

digital video surveillance cameras, plexiglass, and other precautionary measures. So, I just wanted to know if you have a list of what other precautionary measures could be.
So, I'll pass to Deputy Chief in case there's.

So, our Crime Prevention Officers frequently educate our businesses in the business districts, and we partner up and we speak about best practices as far as de-escalation, site surveys, positioning of cameras, things of that nature, and then also positioning of merchandise within the establishment. So, that's the kind of stuff we educate the businesses on how to do it to prevent. Also, key indicators of someone who is shoplifting. So, we do these partnerships. Sometimes the BIDs have ambassadors that we work alongside with. So, these are the measures we take place to safeguard the businesses.
I appreciate that. Since plexiglass is listed, what circumstances would plexiglass be deemed appropriate?
I can't speak to that.
From your experience just as a police officer.
I guess if that's a safeguard that the business wants to put in place to safeguard their employees or the owners, and this is something they want to put in place, I wouldn't.
What exactly would plexiglass protect from?
It could be violence. It could be a sharp object or someone striking the employee. Maybe that's what they want to prevent.
And in your experience, have you seen it to be a successful deterrent?
In some cases, it does. It definitely safeguards the employees. I mean, it's logical, and I think it makes the employees feel safe. That would be a decision they would have to make.
Is there, by chance, any data on the effectiveness of plexiglass?
Not that I know of.
No? Okay. Can you share some of the crime prevention methods the NYPD has used in regard to retail theft?

So, there's many methods that we do use, just so I don't miss anything. First and foremost, the timeliness of reporting. We want these businesses, when the act is happening, to call us immediately. We educate them on how to gather details of the crime and how to report it, how to internally document the incident so to identify trends, recidivist offenders. We also teach them how to de-escalate these incidents. We don't want them acting like the police. We want to get there quickly and prevent it from escalating into a robbery or someone being harmed. We talk about the anti-theft equipment that they use, whether it's RFID chips or trackers, things like that, so we understand what they're using, which could, in turn, help us. And then we talk about their role in prosecution, as well as we talk site surveys, positioning of merchandise, positioning of cameras, and then have a system to communicate across the businesses

themselves. So, if you're in a business district, hey, we just got hit by a group of individuals, look out, this just happened, and they're sharing in real time, whether that be by text message, email, and they're communicating. The businesses are protecting each other, and in turn, we're involved in that communication in some cases. So, there's a lot of best practices going on, and it's definitely assisting us in the complaints.
Do you have data that would identify what some of these high crime areas (TIMER CHIME) or neighborhoods would be, by chance?

So, currently in 2026, we're looking at a couple of commands that just have raw number, large numbers of retail theft across the city, Midtown South. We're talking around 34th Street. That has probably the highest in the city as far as raw number and retail theft, followed by the 13th precinct. We're talking around Union Square area. That's a high number as well in the first precinct down by Houston, Canal Street, Church, Broadway. 52 precinct is particularly high on Fordham

Road. 84 by the Barclays is high for Brooklyn. And then when we talk about Queens, we're looking at Queens Boulevard, Queen Center Mall, Roosevelt Avenue, and the Staten Island Mall. If you want to talk across all the boroughs, those are our high number drivers. So, strategically, that's where we deploy our officers. We have retail theft teams. The commands are able to create conditions teams to deal with this retail theft and/or we have officers on foot, our newer officers in these areas to prevent that theft.
Thank you, Council Member. Next, we have Council Member Banks.

Thank you, Chairs. First of all, I want to back up when the question was asked about the panic buttons. There was a number that was thrown out citywide, the amount of panic buttons that have been installed. Can you give me that number again?

Sure, Council Member. So, the Economic Development Corporation led

this program and worked with the United Bodega Association. They've installed 302 panic buttons.
302. Is there a breakdown per Council District of how many of these panic buttons have been installed?
The Economic Development Corporation would have that. We don't have that.
So, you don't have that. Okay. And as far as resources for the local businesses, what resources are currently in place to support local businesses when it comes to theft prevention?

I know that we're really grateful for local precincts and crime prevention officers on the ground at local precincts who are able to go to small businesses and they're able to do security assessments of the business owner and recommend best practices to business owners. That's one resource that exists currently on retail theft in particular.
Let me take a deeper dive into some of the data. Actually, hopefully you can provide me with some of these numbers. What percentage of the retail theft incidents involve young folks or youth?
I'd have to get back to you on that one. I don't have that.
You don't have that?
No. I don't have that. Sorry.
Are you aware of any diversion programs that may exist that are implemented to assist young folks in preventing these crimes or repeat offenders?

We have a lot of officers that are engaged with the youth. Our Youth Coordination Officers as well as our Explorer program. We have a lot of engagement with the youth that we help guide them away from retail theft.

Okay. And how is the Administration including SBS supporting merchants' associations or Business Improvement

Districts citywide to coordinate anti-theft strategies and potentially invest in shared security tools? What's currently? Because you spoke, but I want to know is there anything else?

So, I think one important thing for us to highlight would be it's been really, really powerful to see Mayor Mamdani on day 14 within two weeks announce Executive Order 11, which directed a range of regulatory agencies to start reviewing, inventorying, and start identifying fines and fees the City government can initiate reductions on to help small businesses thrive and help reduce the burden of small businesses.
When is that going to be completed?

So, there's a range of milestones in that executive order. My understanding is in July, Members of the Council and Members of the State Legislature will receive a package from the Administration, which will include all the reforms that require City Council or State Legislature action. Separate from that requirement, anything that the City could do on its own through

administrative rulemaking or departmental policy, the City Administration will undertake.

I know recently there's been a rash of what they call these takeovers, where you have some young folks who have been going into certain malls, and they've been doing this, they're having this sporadic type of where they're snatching equipment and raiding the stores. In those particular situations, what has been the partnership between local community-based organizations to help prevent some of these occurrences from taking place?

So, a lot of precincts have a strong communication chain with the business districts and the businesses themselves. Like I said before, we have a lot of strong presence in the business districts, and we have direct lines of communication. So, for instance, when we had one of those incidents that you referred to up in Bay Plaza, we were present, and we immediately had officers mobilized and came to aid of those businesses at the Bay Plaza up in the Bronx. So, that disorder or theft is not tolerated, and we'll get the resources over

there. And if the business owners or employees are seeing an issue, they have direct lines of communication with us, and we'll respond as (TIMER CHIME) quickly as possible.

And if the Chair may indulge me, one last question. As far as notification, was there any prior notification given to any of the businesses when the incident had taken place up in the Bronx? And I know Kings Plaza was also threatened, and also in my District, Gateway Mall was also threatened.
I would have to get back to you on those specific incidents on how that communication happened and timeline of it.
All right. Thank you.
I have a couple of follow-up questions. I know we are saying retail theft is down, but when we talk about chain stores, theft is up. Am I correct in that?

I don't have it, but you're talking about specific business types. That I

don't have in front of me right now, and I'd have to get back to you on that.
Okay. And then are certain retail sectors, such as pharmacies, cosmetics, apparel, food, disproportionately targeted?
Some of the businesses that we see mostly affected is Target, CVS, Marshalls, those establishments. Those businesses have seen large numbers of retail theft, without question.

I'm going to go back to the original question, and that goes to this decline in terms of if it's because of underreporting. Like I know firsthand, Walgreens, the locks are getting more plentiful so the quality of life and the consumer experience is declining. And a particular one in my District just doesn't even report anymore. So, I'm very curious and would ask that you start to collect data and look, maybe go back to some of those retailer stores when they were at the height of when the numbers were high. Are they still reporting? Are they even still open for

business to really get a truer understanding of if it's actually down or if it's because of underreporting? My question is, which precincts? I know you mentioned certain corridors currently experience the highest retail theft rates.

So, by volume, we're talking about Midtown South, 34th Street, 13th Precinct, Union Square, Fifth Avenue, First Precinct, Houston, Canal, Church and Broadway, 52 Precinct, Fordham Road, 84 Precinct by the Barclays. We're talking about Atlantic, Flatbush and Fulton Street. 112, we're talking about Queens Boulevard. 110, we're talking about Queens Boulevard and the Queens Center Mall. The 109, we're talking about Roosevelt Avenue. And the 121, we're talking about Staten Island Mall. In some of these areas, we have officers directly on foot and we're deploying them and we have strong coordination. I can specifically speak to in the Staten Island Mall. We have a detail that's placed there and we've made significant strides. Staten Island, matter of fact, has the largest decrease in retail theft for a year. They're down 46.2 percent

for the year. So that's strong leadership out in Staten Island and the good work of the police officers on Staten Island.
My final question, are there any disparities in enforcement outcomes across the boroughs?
As far as what?
Like, is police activity and how enforcement is interacted in, say, Staten Island versus the Bronx any different?

I would have to get back to you on the raw numbers of the arrests and where they're occurring, but the raw numbers would be where the complaints are occurring. So, I would say Midtown South has the largest number of retail theft complaints. They're going to have the largest number of arrests. But I would have to get back to you on that data. Historically, Manhattan's affected the most, specifically Manhattan South.
Thank you. Chair Feliz, do you have any additional questions?

Yes. Some additional questions. So, earlier you mentioned this is a conversation that I've had with many different stakeholders. Earlier you mentioned that you work with the DA on different diversion programs. As we know, people commit retail theft due to many reasons. Again, mental health challenges, substance abuse, and then we have those that are doing that basically to make a profit, take goods and then resell them. And again, you mentioned that you work with the DA on diversion programs. I think one thing that we could all agree on is that those that are committing retail theft due to mental health challenges or substance abuse, we have to make sure that we get them the help that they need so that we could hopefully put an end to the retail theft. I'm just curious, any other way that we've been able to get individuals some type of help without going through the DAs? Any other agencies involved that don't specifically have to route the case towards the DA?

We work with many City agencies, whether it's Department of Homeless

Services. There's a lot of different City agencies that we engage our communities with. So, if we can help connect them to resources, we certainly do that. We work with the business districts and their ambassadors. Their ambassadors are a big help. So, there's many different City agencies that we work with to combat this retail theft.
What are some of the steps that you've seen where other agencies get involved and help resolve the challenge? Any cases that stand out?

I would say in the Bronx, we have a lot of the harm reduction non-profits come out. I saw a lot of their assistance in this matter with those who were drug addicted, substance abuse, that were driving some of our crime along Fordham Road. So, there's non-profits we're working with. We're also working with other City agencies.

What percent of retail theft would you say is due to organized retail theft versus other reasons? I know you said most of them aren't due to organized, but do you have an

estimate of how much of it is due to organized retail theft?
I don't.
(INAUDIBLE) 20 percent? Any rough guess?
I don't have that. I don't have that number.

Okay. So, on retail theft, as we know, it was a major problem during the coronavirus pandemic. We've made some progress. Would you say retail theft affected all commercial corridors equally, or were there some that were more affected than others? And if yes, did we notice any trends?
You're asking me what corridors did I see that are most affected?
Or did we see, are there any factors that we saw stand out in terms of which commercial corridors were being affected more than others?
I would say that…
I'm sure, for example, the busier commercial corridors, more businesses, so.

And like I said, there's certain businesses that are definitely suffering more. Target, CVS, Marshalls, those businesses, the pharmacies. So, types of businesses are being affected, and certain corridors like Fordham Road, Roosevelt Avenue, I spoke of. So those are our hot spots.

What percent of retail theft would you guess, and I say guess because there's no way of getting data on this, but would you guess goes unreported? Would you say one-third of retail theft? Based on the conversations you've had, I'm sure you and your team have worked with different BIDs, different businesses, you've heard directly from them. So, just wondering if there's anything that you consistently get where they say basically, hey, we don't report 80 percent of our cases.

No. I can't speak to that. I wouldn't have that number. But that's one of our best practices, and when we go out and we engage

the businesses, we want them to call us for assistance so we can address this issue.

Okay. And also briefly moving on to a topic that we haven't talked much about today, but this is a conversation that all of us have had for years now. We've talked about panic buttons, especially specifically in our bodegas. What is the NYPD's position on panic buttons? I know based on what I've heard from different Members, it's a good idea, but there's been some challenges with getting it implemented for many different reasons. So, just wondering if you could talk to us about panic buttons in general and the NYPD's position.
Yeah, I don't want to get ahead of the Department. I don't want to speak on that position.

Okay. Cool. All right, well, all right. I don't have any more questions, and of course, I want to make sure that we hear from those that have joined to testify. I just want to thank both of you for all the work that you do on this issue, and of course,

retail theft is extremely complex. We have retail theft challenges due to organized crime, people specifically doing that to make a profit. but then we have others that are using it or engaging in that due to mental health issues, other needs. We need to make sure we get those individuals the help they need so that we can put an end to it. But two things could be true at the same time. We could make sure that we have programs to make sure that we resolve those challenges that they have so that they don't commit retail theft again. But at the same time, we could make sure that we don't ignore the issue because this is a problem that has real life consequences. I remember when I first took office, which was in the middle of the pandemic, speaking with workers from a chain store. There was this young college student who basically said, my first job, my first day on the job, basically somebody took out a knife on her because she basically started speaking with somebody who was committing retail theft. So, this has real life consequences. This isn't just somebody taking an item and going away. This has real life consequences. And, of course, workers deserve to feel safe in their

workplace. And, of course, generally the areas that are affected are areas that are suffering from challenges related to poverty. But this is basically a double-edged sword. These businesses are also creating jobs to help put food on the table for these families that are suffering from poverty. So, it's all about drawing a proper balance to make sure that those that have challenges, we get them the help they need. But at the same time, not create conditions and ignore problems that are making poor people worse off. So, I just want to thank you all for the for all the work you do. And I don't have any more questions. I'll pass it back to the Co-Chair.
Thank you. SBS, I just have two quick things for you. Has SBS done a cost assessment on the implementation on the two bills?
A cost assessment?
Yes.
I think it's 11 million for the first bill, Intro. 553. It's 13.5 million for 623.
Okay. Thank you. And then real quick, how many BIDs have public safety programs, and how does SBS and NYPD engage with them?

We engage very closely with the BID network. We help oversee the BIDs. We have a seat on the board of directors of each of these Business Improvement Districts. I know the NYPD has their own relationships, local precincts up to the borough command and 1PP with business improvement districts. Of the Business Improvement Districts that exist, there's roughly 78. We know 37, so almost half of the network, have their own public safety programs. And that includes things like ambassadors, public safety ambassadors that they have either on their staff or contracted and/or things like pedestrian plaza security cameras that they've deployed to help keep their neighborhoods safe.
Got it. Thank you. Thank you both for your testimony.
Thank you so much.

I now open the hearing for public testimony. I remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have three minutes to speak on today's oversight hearing topic, Retail Theft, or on the bills on our agenda. Intro. 553 or Intro. 623. Additionally, the bills we are hearing today aim to improve safety… Oh, I will now turn it over to Chair Feliz. My apologies.

If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant-at-Arms. You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of the close of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. For in-person panelists, please come up to the table once your name has been called. Now I will call our first in-person panel. Matthew Barr, Kelsey Bobersky, and Frank Garcia. Is Matthew here? Matthew Barr. Kelsey, you may begin.

Thank you. Good afternoon, Chairs Feliz and Thomas-Henry and honorable Committee Members. My name is Kelsey Dorado Bobersky, and I am the Director of State and Local Government Relations for the Retail Council of New York State. Our organization is the state's leading trade group for the retail industry, representing member stores in New York City and across the state, ranging from the smallest independent merchants to

national and international brands. Thank you for the opportunity to speak today on retail theft prevention and Introductions 553 and 623. Store and community safety is our organization's top priority, and it has been for years. Our work in this space is focused on organized retail crime syndicates and those engaging in habitual retail theft. This criminal activity goes well beyond the obvious financial loss for retailers. It is a serious issue that compromises the safety of store employees and customers. At the State level, we joined the Governor, the Attorney General, and lawmakers in 2024 to support and advance new laws and related funding to address the rise in retail theft. These efforts have proven to be effective, as Governor Hochul in August announced that retail theft has declined across New York. In New York City, the Retail Council has partnered with elected officials, District Attorneys, the NYPD, businesses, and community groups through the New York City Retail Theft Task Force. The effective and consistent collaboration among dozens of participants at each meeting cannot be understated. Since the first

meeting at Gracie Mansion in December 2023, retail theft has been added to the COMPStat report, giving local businesses and communities the data necessary to respond in a meaningful way. According to the most recent COMPStat report on February 22nd, retail theft has declined 24.2 percent since 2024. We strongly encourage Mayor Mamdani to continue the work of this task force with the support of the City Council. The progress that has been made to date is important to promote a safe and enjoyable shopping experience for residents and tourists alike. As it relates to the bills being heard today, the Retail Council supports each bill as they would offer valuable assistance to small stores throughout New York City. We are more than willing to partner with the City Council and designated agencies to promote the programs should the bills be approved. Thank you again for the opportunity to testify, and I look forward to answering any questions you may have.
Thank you, Kelsey. I do have a couple of questions.
Sure.
You mentioned the Retail Task Force. Where does the Retail Theft Task Force currently operate from, and how can we support its continuation?

The task force sat under the Department of Public Safety under the former administration. We have not met thus far, so its placement is in a little bit of limbo at the moment. And any support in terms of, you know, advocating for the task force to continue would be greatly appreciated.
And what are the current trends in retail theft? Have you seen them change over time, or what should a business look out for?

Sure. That's a great question. We saw a spike, as was previously mentioned, kind of post-COVID with smash and grabs and organized groups going into stores. That aspect has declined slightly. We're seeing a larger uptick as it relates to gift card fraud, which is essentially groups of people going in and stealing gift cards that are unpurchased from stores, bringing

them to a third location, tampering with those gift cards, and then bringing them back to locations. So, when a consumer purchases the gift card, the funds on it are immediately drained. We worked very closely with Senator Krueger's office in the State Senate on a bill that would address this issue. The Senate approved it last year. It didn't make it in the Assembly, but that's a focus for us this year.
And what can we do to further decrease the rate of retail theft?

Continue the task force. I really can't emphasize enough how wonderful the collaboration between all the stakeholders has been. All five District Attorneys participate in the task force. Our organization, individual businesses, Business Improvement Districts, a variety of City agencies. It really is a wonderful avenue, especially for small businesses, to get the resources that they need and up-to-date information. Like I said, retail theft has declined almost 25 percent since 2024. The task force was started in December of 2023. It's really been a phenomenal resource, and we really need it to continue.
And my final question is can you describe the impact retail theft has had on both consumers and businesses?

Sure. I think there's a little bit of overlap there, especially when it comes to things. I know they were previously mentioned, like items being locked up at stores. That is not something that stores want to do. Unfortunately, if there are some items that are not locked up, they simply will not be there for consumers to purchase. So that is a direct impact on both businesses and consumers. Of course, when we talk about the business impact, we cannot forget the worker impact. It can be incredibly traumatic to witness a retail theft event, especially if there is violence associated with it. Retail is many people's first jobs, so they come in at 16, 17, 18 years old and experience this, and it's incredibly traumatizing. Additionally, from the consumer perspective, I would be remiss if I didn't acknowledge the consumer protection aspect of this. If items are being stolen and then resold, there is a

concern if the packaging of those items is damaged, if those items are expired or tampered with. And this is especially concerning when it comes to over-the-counter medications, food, personal care products, and things like electronic devices. If you're going to steal and sell a drill, somebody could get it and the cord could be frayed. There could be an issue with it that makes the product unsafe. So, if consumers are going online and unknowingly purchasing stolen equipment and stolen products, it can be incredibly dangerous.
One final question. I know you guys have a lot of members, and we've seen a lot of store closures. How much of that have any of your members, if any, attributed to retail theft?

It's certainly a factor. I would not say that it's the sole factor in store closures, but we have seen some across the country. This is not a New York or a New York City-specific problem, but theft is certainly a factor when it comes to store closures.

Thank you.

Chair Feliz?

Yeah. Just one brief question. Thank you so much for everything that you do for our small businesses and our city and state. Just curious, what steps have you seen businesses take to reduce these problems?

Many. I think it very much depends on the individual business and what is best for their store. There's no one who knows a store better than the store owner and the people who work in it. So, whenever we talk about preventative measures or what stores should be doing, it's important that we always include the flexibility for stores to make those decisions for themselves and what would benefit them best. That can include everything from plexiglass, items being behind a locked container, cameras. It really runs the gamut of what is going to work best for individual stores.
All right. Thank you.
Thank you.
Any other questions? Okay. Thank you. Mr. Garcia.

Madam Chair, thank you for having me speak. My name is Frank Garcia. I'm Chairman of the National Association of Latino State Chambers. I'm also the outgoing Chairman of the New York State Chamber of Commerce and just became this week the first President of the Multicultural Business Coalition representing 80 percent of the minority chambers, the Korean, the Asian. The national supermarket is part of us, the Latino restaurant, Francisco from the Bodega Association. I know Mr. Chair Feliz knows us very well with the issue of Jose Alba. He was there and helped us with the issue when we dealed with the issue of one of our bodegas almost losing his life and going to jail for defending himself. So, this is an issue that's really affecting our members. It hurts me to hear some of the comments from the NYPD about the panic buttons. You can't call the NYPD when someone's robbing you. And so to have a panic button, and I thank our Chair

who's Latino who understands the bodegas and understands our community to bring that out in a panic button because I know the supermarkets have been very clear with him. Anthony Pena, the new President, Francisco, and also the Association of Bodega has been very clear they need a panic button. And when all these organizations are coming together, both bodegas, saying the same thing, we need to listen. And so, Madam Chair, I haven't had the opportunity to meet you, but it's important to give us a voice. We don't have a voice right now. What's going on with the federal government, normally our members when they buy a bodega or restaurant or supermarket, they would get funding through the SBA. Now if you're a green card holder and 50 percent of immigrant businesses are green card holders will not be able to get loans, that means we will not be able to afford cameras or anything or panic buttons. Before we would have that, Jose Alba's, and you're talking about the Arab counterparts too, that will not be able to also afford it because they're green card holders too. So, this is bigger than just one minute, three minutes for me to tell you. We are

having a meeting with the Speaker with all 75 presidents, but we picked 25 to meet with the Speaker at 3 o'clock where we could let you know individually. A lot of Chambers didn't want to come today because when you speak against SBS, you get blackballed like I did. I was there supporting small minority business with certification with the pandemic. I've been on that board since Bill de Blasio. To this day, I haven't been invited to the board no more. Why? Because I've been speaking up in issues like this, issue of payments for MBEs, issues with certifications taking us a year and a half. For SBS to be in charge of giving the cameras, I feel they will only give it to those that are (TIMER CHIME) influential and not those small businesses, bodegas, that are risking their life and every day have to deal with these issues. Thank you.
No. Thank you for your testimony, and I will say you do have an ally in me. So please, if you have any recommendations, please continue on.

We have our press conference next Friday at 10:30 with the Speaker, and

we'd love for you with all 70 presidents for the first time coming together to deal with these issues and other issues that we're facing like the loans.
Okay. And you mentioned the panic buttons. I know that SBS has mentioned that over 300 have been given out.
Not our bodegas, not our members.
Okay. Okay.
I know that for a fact.

Okay. How many members do you have? We have 100,000 members now, including the 35 Latino chambers that each have their own group. The Bodega Association, the Bronx Hispanic Chamber, the LGB Chamber, you know, we have a lot of chambers that are part of us. It's 26 in total, but when you get the other ethnic chambers, we're another 55, including the Koreans, the Indians, the Arabs. The New York Chamber, Mark Jaffe is hosting us right now and putting us all together for the first time.

Out of all these organizations that you represent, do you all

capture any data in terms of how many of your members have gone out of business because of retail theft?

Yes. The local chambers, like the supermarkets who have lobbyists and have money to be able to do that, Francisco from the Bodega Association has got grants to do that. They do have that, and Radames has that, too. And the other organizations, like the Bronx Hispanic Chamber, Bishop Kirkland, who has the worldwide churches, also has done her own survey. So, we do have that information, Madam Chair, and we could give that to you, and we could also discuss it on Tuesday if you could make it at 3 o'clock, our call with the Speaker.
For clarity, I have two different times. I have a 3 o'clock and a 10:30.

3 o'clock is the meeting with the Speaker, and the press conference is next Friday, 10:30 in the morning. We have a private meeting with the Speaker, and Magdalena mentioned that she was going to invite you and Chairman Feliz also to be part of that, and the other Latino Council

people to be part of that because we're going to talk about issues that here we can't talk.
Okay. So, I look forward to those meetings. Chair Feliz.
Yeah. Quick question. Just wanted to get your take on it. So, we've been having the conversation about panic buttons for years.
I know.

And I know people have different ideas about what it means. For some people it means notifying the local precinct about a certain situation happening at a specific bodega, and I know there was a recent program where it would basically notify the local or the nearby store owners. So, what's your position on the panic buttons? How do you think it could be properly implemented, and what would be a good system that would work and would help resolve some of the safety issues?

The panic buttons has to be in different languages, the information, and whoever they hired has to be sensitive. Our Korean counterparts and Chinese are getting equipment they don't know how to install because of language. And so, we need to be sensitive to that, especially with the panic buttons and working with all the ethnic chambers that deal with these communities. I think it's important to have an advisory board for the City Council like Robert Jackson had when he was head of the Committee. That way we could not depend on SBS' advisory board and be able to explain these issues and give you those things directly us. And there's no middleman. There's no lobbyist. We could tell you every two months. I know that Congresswoman Yvette, I was in her thing. We've spoken many a times when we had, we only speak when there's issues like Jose Alba. I think we need to speak more to be able to have a voice because I know with the Speaker as a business owner and some of the Council here are former business owners, you know the pain. Did I answer your question?

Good afternoon, Chairs and Committee Members. My name is Alissa Johnson, and I'm a Legal Fellow with the Surveillance Technology Oversight Project, or STOP. STOP is a New York-based civil rights and anti-surveillance group that advocates and litigates against discriminatory surveillance. STOP also shares the concerns expressed previously in this hearing about live sharing of camera feeds with law enforcement and the need for strict guardrails around data collection, retention, and sharing. Biometric surveillance in public spaces, including grocery stores and other retail outlets, puts our privacy and civil liberties at risk without making stores meaningfully safer. The recent public outcry around deployment of facial recognition technology at Wegmans stores shows that New Yorkers strongly object

to being surveilled as they buy their groceries and go about their day, and for good reason. First, our biometrics are immutable. Once a retail chain, like Wegmans, collects our face scan, that data poses a persistent risk to our privacy. If a person's credit information is stolen, they can contact their bank and mitigate that risk by getting reissued a new card, for example. But if our biometric data is sold to a third party, or shared with law enforcement, or stolen by a malicious cyber actor, that data is compromised forever. Second, biometric surveillance reinforces racial and socioeconomic inequities. As the FTC found in its 2023 ruling banning Rite Aid's use of facial recognition technology, these tools are less accurate in identifying women and people of color. Uneven deployment of biometric surveillance in quote-unquote high-risk, high shoplifting risk areas also disproportionately targets New Yorkers at or near the poverty line, people who may only have access to a single grocery store and are less likely to be able to access alternatives such as online shopping, as

they may not be banked or have access to a permanent address. And third, getting flagged by a biometric surveillance system can have devastating consequences. Ranging from embarrassment and harassment to outright denial of service. Even if such technologies were completely accurate, they impose disproportionate penalties for minor property crimes and extend the long arm of the criminal justice system. All of us deserve to buy food without being tracked every moment by New York's sprawling surveillance dragnet. And shoplifting once, as an 18-year-old, shouldn't prevent someone from buying food, or going to a concert, or entering their own apartment building. For these reasons, STOP urges the City Council to amend these introductions to explicitly exclude funding for security systems implementing biometric surveillance tools, included but not limited to face, gait, and voice recognition. schools and grocery stores, and our federal government has demonstrated the desire and capacity to retaliate against protesters for constitutionally protected speech, we also ask the City Council to urge State Legislators to pass several bills aimed at prohibiting the use of biometric surveillance throughout the public sphere. S-5609, to ban the use of biometric surveillance by (TIMER CHIME) law enforcement; S-2478, to prohibit face surveillance by landlords on any residential premises; S-7135, to ban biometric surveillance in places of public accommodation; and S-3827, to prohibit biometric surveillance in schools.
